rounds.text: Alfa Ica (India) Ltd is currently trading at a significant discount to its intrinsic value, with a margin of safety calculated at 45.1% [E44]. The market is failing to price in the company's recent operational momentum, as evidenced by a 38% growth in sales and a 70% surge in profit over the trailing twelve months [E17, E21]. This valuation disconnect is highlighted by a P/E ratio of 11.93x and an EV/EBITDA of 6.84x, both of which are substantially lower than their respective sector benchmarks of 21.96x and 12.25x [E6, E11]. Furthermore, the company demonstrates robust financial health through a cash conversion ratio of 3.00x, confirming that reported profits are fully backed by actual cash flow [E34]. Conceded: the company has delivered poor long-term sales growth [E52], a low return on equity [E53], and currently offers a dividend yield of 0.00% [E4]. Despite these historical drags, the current reverse DCF analysis suggests the market is pricing in a contraction of 1.2% in earnings, which stands in stark contrast to the company's accelerating performance [E45, E62].

Alfa Ica (India) Ltd exhibits structurally sluggish long-term growth and chronically weak capital efficiency, reflected by a 10-year compounded profit growth of just 4% [E18] and a 10-year median return on equity of only 8% [E26]. Shareholder returns have stagnated alongside these fundamentals, with the stock delivering a 1-year price decline of -9% [E25] and a meager 3% compounded share price growth over 10 years [E22]. Furthermore, the business refuses to return capital to its owners despite reporting repeated profits, resulting in a dividend yield of 0.00% [E4, E51]. Operating performance is deteriorating at the margin, evidenced by operating margins compressing by 2 percentage points over the trailing twelve months compared to three years earlier [E30], alongside an inconsistent margin trend [E32]. Debt has also crept upward to Rs 18 Cr in September 2026 from Rs 17 Cr a year prior [E38], while the company's reported earnings are propped up by non-operating sources, specifically including Rs 2.23 Cr of other income [E54]. Conceded: the company has demonstrated strong near-term momentum with trailing twelve-month sales and profit growth surging by 38% and 70% respectively [E17, E21], and its return on assets underperforms the sector benchmark [E8].

Conceded: 10-year compounded profit growth is 4% [E18], 10-year median ROE is 8% [E26], 1-year share price growth is -9% [E25], 10-year share price growth is 3% [E22], dividend yield is 0.00% [E4], and operating margins have compressed by 2 percentage points over three years [E30] with inconsistent trends [E32]. However, the bear fixates entirely on stale historical averages while ignoring a fundamental business inflection, evidenced by TTM sales growth surging by 38% and TTM profit growth accelerating by 70% [E17, E21]. Furthermore, recent results are scoring an exceptional 98 out of 100 on improving fundamentals, proving that judging this turnaround on stagnant past sentiment is entirely premature [E62]. While borrowings ticked up to Rs 18 Cr [E38], the company generated robust operating cash flow of Rs 6 Cr and free cash flow of Rs 4 Cr in March 2026, backed by a stellar 3.00x cash conversion rate that fully supports reported profits [E34, E35, E36]. Finally, the bear's concern over Rs 2.23 Cr of other income [E54] is heavily outweighed by the massive scale of operational expansion and a discounted cash flow valuation showing a substantial 45.1% margin of safety against the current market price [E43, E44].

Conceded: TTM sales grew 38% and TTM profit grew 70% [E17, E21], and operating cash flow reached Rs 6 Cr with a 3.00x cash conversion [E34, E35]. However, dismissing 10-year historical averages as stale [E18, E26] ignores the reality of long-term mediocrity, where compounded profit growth over a decade crawls at just 4% and the 10-year median ROE languishes at 8%. The glowing 98 out of 100 results score and operational expansion arguments [E62] must be tempered by the fact that earnings are artificially inflated by Rs. 2.23 Cr of other income [E54]. Furthermore, the bull leans heavily on a discounted cash flow margin of safety [E43, E44] while ignoring that the underlying business model suffers from structural margin compression, with operating margins dropping by 2 percentage points over three years to 4% and exhibiting persistently inconsistent trends [E30, E32]. Finally, despite ticking borrowings up to Rs 18 Cr [E38] and generating free cash flow [E36], the company rewards shareholders with a 0.00% dividend yield [E4] alongside a poor 5-year sales growth rate of 9.45% [E52] and a depressed 3-year average ROE of 7.41% [E53].
